A splinter is a small, thin, sharp piece that has broken off or separated from a larger solid object. Think of it as a fragment — but not just any fragment. A splinter is specifically thin, needle-like, and usually pointed at one or both ends. That sharp, shard-like shape is what makes a splinter a splinter, and not just a "piece" or "chunk."

Imagine snapping a dry stick in half. Along the broken edge, you might notice tiny, thin, sharp needles of wood sticking out or falling off. Those are splinters. They are:

  • Long and narrow (not blocky or round)
  • Sharp at the tip (like a tiny spike or needle)
  • Thin (sometimes thin enough to be nearly invisible)
  • Small (usually just a few millimetres to a couple of centimetres long)

Wood is by far the most common source, but splinters can come from almost any hard, brittle material that breaks apart in a sharp, shard-like way:

  • Wood — rough wooden planks, old furniture, tree bark, wooden fences
  • Glass — shattered glass breaks into thin, razor-sharp splinters
  • Metal — certain metals, when fractured, produce fine, sharp fragments
  • Bone — in medical situations, a broken bone can produce splinters
  • Plastic — hard, brittle plastics can snap into shard-like splinters
The Most Familiar Scenario — A Splinter in Your Skin

This is where most people first encounter the word. If you run your hand along a rough, unfinished wooden surface — an old park bench, a wooden plank, a fence — a tiny pointed sliver of wood can pierce your skin and get stuck underneath it. That is a splinter.

It sits just below the surface of your skin, you can sometimes see it, and it causes a sharp, stinging pain, especially when you press on that spot. Getting it out usually requires a pair of tweezers or a needle. Almost everyone has experienced this, which is why "splinter" is so strongly associated with wood and skin.
Splinters in a Wider Physical Sense

Beyond skin and wood, you will also hear "splinter" used for any thin, sharp fragment of a shattered hard material. For example:

  • When a glass window shatters violently, splinters of glass fly outward.
  • A bomb or explosion can send splinters of metal (also called shrapnel) in all directions.
  • A falling mirror might leave splinters scattered across the floor.

In all these cases, the key idea is the same: a thin, sharp, dangerous fragment that has broken off from something solid.
The Figurative Meaning — When "Splinter" Describes Groups or Organizations

This is where the word moves beyond the physical world. Just as a splinter breaks away from a larger piece of wood, the word "splinter" is used to describe a small group of people that breaks away from a larger group, usually because of disagreements or differences in beliefs.

This usage gives rise to the very common phrase "splinter group" — a faction that separates itself from a larger organization, political party, religion, or movement.

After years of internal conflict, a small splinter group broke away from the main political party and formed their own.

The religious splinter group rejected the teachings of the main church.

The image is deliberate and powerful — just like a physical splinter, these groups are smaller, sharper (in their views), and separated from the main body.
Quick Summary of All Its Meanings

SenseIn Simple Terms
Physical (most common)A small, thin, sharp piece broken off from a larger solid object (wood, glass, metal, etc.)
MedicalA sharp fragment lodged under the skin
FigurativeA small group that has broken away from a larger one

• She winced as she pulled a splinter from her thumb.
  • The wooden floor was old and full of splinters.
  • Splinters of glass covered the pavement after the car accident.
  • A splinter of the original movement formed their own independent group.
  • He used tweezers to carefully remove the splinter embedded in his heel.

If you ever need to recall the word fast: a splinter is a thin, sharp, pointed fragment — most often wood — that has broken away from something larger, sometimes embedding itself painfully in skin, and (figuratively) any small, sharp faction that breaks off from a larger whole.
